corrected_fields.summary: This paper extends the Store of Value Circulation Reserve (SCR) theory of inflation by examining whether reservation inflation—the real appreciation of nominal claims relative to goods—can arise during a hard-money era when circulation inflation (CPI) is negative. Using British retail price data and U.S. historical CPI, the author finds that between 1873-1896, while prices fell from 18.0 to 14.7 in Britain and 36.0 to 25.0 in the U.S., a fixed-claim reservation index rose 22.4% in Britain and 44.0% in the U.S. The paper argues hard money does not eliminate inflationary pressure but relocates it from consumer prices to nominal claim values.
corrected_fields.why_it_matters: This historical case study challenges simplistic hard-money narratives by showing that gold-standard deflation did not eliminate inflationary pressure but transformed its expression from consumer prices to nominal claim values. The findings suggest CPI alone may understate monetary-material asymmetry during reserve-dominant regimes.
